denti-e-gengive-sani.title: How to keep teeth and gums healthy
denti-e-gengive-sani.excerpt: Five habits that make far more difference than any treatment. None of them takes more than three minutes a day.

body.v: Oral health depends far less on what we do at the practice than people think, and far more on what happens during the 364 days we do not see you. The good news is that the variables that really matter are few.
1. The space between the teeth is where problems start

A toothbrush, however good, reaches three of the five surfaces of every tooth. The two interproximal ones — those in contact with the neighbouring teeth — stay uncovered, and that is exactly where most decay and gum inflammation begins. Floss or an interdental brush, once a day, is worth more than any toothpaste.
2. Technique matters more than force

Brushing hard does not clean better: it wears away enamel at the necks of the teeth and makes gums recede. The correct direction is from gum towards tooth, with short movements and soft bristles. If you use an electric brush, rest it in place and let it work without scrubbing.
3. The right moment to brush
After something acidic — citrus, vinegar, fizzy drinks, white wine — enamel is temporarily softened. Brushing straight away abrades it. Better to rinse with water and wait twenty or thirty minutes.
4. Bleeding is not normal

A healthy gum does not bleed, not even when you floss. If it bleeds, there is inflammation. The most common mistake is to stop cleaning that area because it bleeds: the result is the exact opposite of what is needed. In most cases, careful cleaning resolves the bleeding within a week.
5. Recall is not a commercial ritual

Interproximal decay and early periodontitis give no symptoms. By the time they do, the treatment needed is an order of magnitude more complex. Regular recall exists to catch them while they are still small, and the interval should be calibrated to individual risk: not everyone needs the same frequency.
The best treatment is the one that never had to happen.
If it has been more than twelve months since your last check-up, it is time to book one. Not because there is certainly something wrong, but because that is the only way to know.

v.text: Worthington HV et al., «Home use of interdental cleaning devices, in addition to toothbrushing, for preventing and controlling periodontal diseases and dental caries», Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2019
Fee PA et al., «Recall intervals for oral health in primary care patients», Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2020

implantologia-cosa-sapere.title: Dental implants: what to know beforehand
implantologia-cosa-sapere.excerpt: The questions patients rarely ask, and which they should always ask, before having an implant placed.

body.v: The dental implant is a reliable procedure, with success rates the literature places above 95% at ten years. Precisely because it has become routine, it is worth understanding what that 95% depends on.
It is not the screw, it is the plan

The position of the implant must be determined by the restoration it will support, not by the bone that happens to be there. This is what separates an implant that lasts decades from one that causes problems: an implant placed where it was convenient, rather than where it was needed, produces a restoration that is hard to clean — and what cannot be cleaned becomes inflamed.
The CT scan is not optional

A panoramic radiograph is two-dimensional and distorted. Cone beam tomography shows the real thickness of the bone, the position of the inferior alveolar nerve and of the maxillary sinus. Planning on a panoramic means discovering in theatre information that could have been had beforehand.
Peri-implantitis exists, and is preventable

It is the equivalent of periodontitis around the implant: inflammation and progressive bone loss. It does not hurt and often shows itself late. The main risk factors are untreated periodontitis, smoking, a restoration that cannot be cleaned, and skipped recall appointments. Three of those four depend on decisions made before surgery.
The right questions to ask

v: Is planning carried out on a CT scan and with a surgical guide?
Who makes the restoration, and with what workflow?
What is the maintenance plan after fitting, and how often?
What happens, in practical terms, if the implant does not integrate?

body.v: A practice with precise answers to those four questions very probably has a protocol. And it is the protocol, more than the brand of implant, that determines the result at ten years.
An implant does not end when the crown is fitted: that is where it begins.

v.text: Chrcanovic BR et al., «Long-term (10-year) dental implant survival: a systematic review and sensitivity meta-analysis», Journal of Dentistry, 2019
Dagassan-Berndt D et al., «Implant treatment planning regarding augmentation procedures: panoramic radiographs vs. cone beam computed tomography images», Clinical Oral Implants Research, 2016
«Risk factors for peri-implantitis: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of observational studies», Journal of Dentistry, 2024

sbiancamento-come-funziona.title: Teeth whitening: how it actually works
sbiancamento-come-funziona.excerpt: What happens to enamel during professional whitening, why home remedies disappoint, and how long the result lasts.

body.v: Whitening is probably the dental treatment surrounded by the most misinformation. It is worth being clear about the mechanism, because everything else follows from it.
Nothing is removed

Peroxide passes through the enamel and reaches the pigmented molecules deposited over time in the dentine beneath, breaking them into smaller, colourless ones. There is no abrasion, no removal of tissue: the tooth does not become thinner or weaker.
Why bicarbonate does not work

Bicarbonate, activated charcoal and "whitening" toothpastes work by abrasion: they remove surface stains and do not touch the internal colour of the tooth. The result is modest and, with prolonged use, paid for in worn enamel.
The biological limit

Every tooth has a base colour determined by the dentine, and whitening works within that limit. Two people having the same treatment get different results. Yellow-brown discolouration responds well; greyish shades, often from medication, much less so.
How long it lasts
From one to three years, with wide variation linked to coffee, tea, red wine and smoking. A home top-up of two or three nights once a year maintains the result without repeating the full cycle.

One practical note: if you have fillings or crowns among the visible teeth, remember that they do not whiten. After treatment they may look darker and need replacing, which should be accounted for from the start.

v.text: American Dental Association, «Whitening», ADA Oral Health Topics
«Transenamel and transdentinal penetration of hydrogen peroxide applied to cracked or microabrasioned enamel», Journal of Dentistry, PubMed

prevenzione-controlli-periodici.title: Prevention: why regular check-ups matter
prevenzione-controlli-periodici.excerpt: The two most common diseases of the mouth do not hurt until it is late. That is the whole point of recall.

body.v: Decay and periodontitis share a characteristic that makes them insidious: in the phase when they are easily treated, they give no symptoms at all. Pain arrives when decay has reached the pulp, mobility when the bone already lost is considerable.
What we look for at a check-up

Not only decay. Periodontal probing measures pocket depth and bleeding; examination of the soft tissues looks for mucosal lesions; checking the bite identifies signs of bruxism before the teeth wear down. Bitewing radiographs, every twelve to twenty-four months, show the interproximal decay the eye cannot see.
The right interval is not the same for everyone

Six months is an average, not a rule. Anyone who has had periodontitis, who has implants, whose saliva is less protective or whose diet is acidic needs closer recall. Someone whose mouth has been stable for years can afford longer intervals. Personalising the interval is, in fact, the clinical part of recall.
A question of orders of magnitude

Decay caught early is treated with an adhesive restoration in a single appointment. The same decay, two years later, may require root canal treatment and a crown: five times the chair time, a different financial commitment, and a tooth that is structurally weaker for good.
Prevention is not an add-on service. It is the main work, and everything else is what we do when prevention arrived too late.

v.text: Fee PA et al., «Recall intervals for oral health in primary care patients», Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2020
«Effect of Different Frequencies of Dental Visits on Dental Caries and Periodontal Disease: A Scoping Review», International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2023

devitalizzazione-quando-serve.title: Root canal treatment: when it's needed and what to expect
devitalizzazione-quando-serve.excerpt: What really happens inside the tooth, when root canal treatment is needed and what to expect.

body.v: Root canal treatment has a reputation it no longer deserves. With modern anaesthesia the procedure is no more uncomfortable than a deep filling: the pain that makes people dread it is usually the pain that came before, caused by the inflammation that made treatment necessary.
What happens inside the tooth

At the centre of every tooth is the pulp: living tissue, with nerves and blood vessels, running through a canal from the crown down to the root. When deep decay, a fracture or trauma reaches it, the pulp becomes inflamed and, left untreated, dies. Root canal treatment removes this tissue, disinfects the canal and seals it: the tooth stays in place, but is no longer vital.
Why we work at 20x magnification

Root canals aren't straight tubes: they branch, curve, and sometimes merge into isthmuses that are hard to see with the naked eye. The operating microscope isn't an accessory: it helps the dentist find accessory canals that would otherwise go untreated — the most common cause of failure years later. It's the difference between cleaning a canal and cleaning all of them.
The numbers, honestly

Long-term studies show 97% tooth survival at ten years, declining gradually over subsequent decades — a sign that a treated tooth can last a lifetime, but isn't immune to other problems (new decay, a fracture). For retreatment — when a first attempt, perhaps done elsewhere without a microscope, didn't succeed — success rates are lower, around 77%: one more reason to get it right the first time.
When extraction is worth considering

Root canal treatment isn't always the right choice. A vertically fractured root, a tooth structure too compromised to support a restoration, or insufficient periodontal support can make an implant the more predictable solution. It's a case-by-case judgement, made with an X-ray in hand, not a rule.
A well-treated root canal isn't felt at all: that's the very definition of success.

v.text: Ng YL et al., «Outcomes of primary root canal therapy: an updated systematic review of longitudinal clinical studies published between 2003 and 2020», International Endodontic Journal
«Long-term tooth survival and success following primary root canal treatment: a 5- to 37-year retrospective observation», Clinical Oral Investigations, 2023

parodontite-non-solo-gengive.title: Periodontitis: not just a gum problem
parodontite-non-solo-gengive.excerpt: Untreated gum disease doesn't stop at the teeth: research links it to cardiovascular risk and diabetes control. What the evidence actually says.

body.v: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammation that progressively destroys the bone around the teeth. It doesn't hurt until it's advanced, which makes it easy to ignore — but research in recent years has made clear that its consequences don't stop at the mouth.
How it's treated, first of all

The baseline treatment isn't surgical: it's scaling and root planing, a thorough mechanical clean below the gumline that removes bacterial biofilm and calculus from the root surfaces. It remains the most effective treatment for most cases, with measurable improvements in pocket depth and bleeding. Surgery only comes into play for the deepest pockets, when scaling alone isn't enough.
The link with diabetes

The relationship runs both ways: chronic high blood sugar worsens periodontal inflammation, and untreated periodontitis in turn worsens glycaemic control. Diabetic patients with periodontitis have up to six times the risk of poor glycaemic control compared with those with healthy gums. Treating the gums, in a diabetic patient, is also a measure of metabolic control.
The link with the heart

Chronic inflammation and the presence of periodontal bacteria in the bloodstream are associated with increased cardiovascular risk, estimated at two to three times higher in the most severe forms. This doesn't mean periodontitis causes a heart attack: it means it's an additional risk factor, of the same order as others already routinely monitored.
What this means in practice

It isn't a reason for alarm, it's one more reason not to put off a periodontal check-up — especially with a family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease. Periodontitis is detected with a simple, painless probing that should be part of every routine check-up.
Bleeding gums aren't a cosmetic detail: they're a signal worth listening to.

v.text: Sanz M et al., «Association between periodontal diseases and cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and respiratory diseases: consensus report EFP/WONCA Europe», Journal of Clinical Periodontology, 2023
«Dental Scaling and Root Planing for Periodontal Health: A Review of the Clinical Effectiveness, Cost-effectiveness, and Guidelines», CADTH / NCBI Bookshelf
